devo-036.title: Cladoxylopsid trees grow the first forests
devo-036.text:
At the start of the Devonian, plants stood about 30 cm tall. By its end, the tallest reached 30 m. Somewhere in between, Earth grew its first forests.

The pioneers were cladoxylopsid trees, which formed the first forests in Earth history during the Eifelian. Trees over eight meters tall had appeared by the Middle Devonian, and the earliest known fossil forest dates from the Eifelian. Cladoxylopsids were not alone. Lower, shrub-like forests of lycophytes, horsetails, ferns and progymnosperms spread too.

The leap to height happened more than once. By the late Givetian, three separate groups had evolved tree-like forms: the cladoxylalean ferns, the lycopsids and the progymnosperms. Height is a race for light, and several lineages joined it at once. The consequences went far beyond the forest floor, because so much new plant matter changed the air, the soils and the rivers, as {{ref:devo-038}} and {{ref:devo-072}} show.

devo-041.title: Sponge and coral reefs flourish
devo-041.text: A Devonian barrier reef in Australia's Kimberley region once stretched 350 km along a continent's edge. Reefs like it were built either by microbes or by stromatoporoids, layered sponges, together with tabulate and rugose corals. Stromatoporoids recovered strongly in the Early and Middle Devonian and peaked in diversity in the Eifelian. Reefs also lined Laurussia's southeast coast, now southern England and Belgium. Climate decided who built them: microbes in warm periods, corals and stromatoporoids in cooler times.

devo-038.title: Forests cool the Middle Devonian
devo-038.text: The new forests did more than shade the ground. They drew carbon out of the air and buried it in sediments, where it could no longer trap heat. That drawdown may be reflected in a Middle Devonian cooling of around 5 °C.

devo-039.title: The progymnosperms appear
devo-039.text: Progymnosperms, plants that came before the seed plants, first appear in the Middle Devonian. The group lasted a long time, into the Lopingian of the late Permian. Their best-known order, the Archaeopteridales, spans the Middle and Late Devonian.

devo-040.title: The Variscan mountains begin to rise
devo-040.text: A mountain belt that would deform crust from Iberia and Ireland to France, Germany and the Czech Republic started to grow in the Middle Devonian. This was the Variscan orogeny, and it continued into the early Permian. Its engine was a set of Armorican terranes, small blocks of crust drifting north. They closed the Rheic Ocean ahead of them and began colliding with southeastern Laurussia. From about 390 million years ago, Rheic seafloor subducted beneath the Mid-German highs south of Laurussia. By the end of the Devonian, all the Armorican terranes were joined to Laurussia.

devo-035.title: The Catskill Delta spreads west
devo-035.text: A wedge of red sandstone up to 3,000 m thick lies under Pennsylvania and New York. Rivers and marshes built it as the Catskill Delta, carrying sediment eroded from the Acadian Mountains west into the inland Kaskaskia Sea. It records large-scale deposition on land during the Acadian orogeny. It also preserves many early tetrapodomorph fishes and land plants, key evidence for how vertebrates moved onto land.

devo-042.title: Zachełmie, the oldest tetrapod tracks
devo-042.text: Some prints in a Polish quarry show toes. The tracks at Zachełmie, from the Eifelian, are the oldest evidence of tetrapods, four-limbed vertebrates. They predate the oldest tetrapod body fossils by about 18 million years. They were made in shallow lagoons on a marine carbonate platform, which supports a tidal-shore origin for land vertebrates. If genuine, they turn Tiktaalik-like elpistostegids into late-surviving relics; the next oldest tracks, about 385 million years old, come from Valentia Island, Ireland. Not everyone agrees they are tracks at all. Some researchers read them as fish feeding traces instead.

devo-043.title: The Kačák event darkens the seas
devo-043.text: Near the end of the Eifelian, the oceans warmed, rose and lost their oxygen. The Kačák event lasted perhaps 200,000 to 700,000 years. High sunlight probably heated the seas, raising sea level as water expanded, and strengthened monsoons that filled Scotland's Achanarras lake, the deepest in the Orcadian Basin. Anoxia, a lack of oxygen, laid down black shales. Open-ocean animals were hit hardest: agoniatitid ammonoids suffered heavy losses while tornoceratids diversified. Warming wrecked the cool-water Malvinoxhosan Realm off Gondwana. Estimates put the loss at about 24% to 32% of marine genera, milder than the Late Devonian extinctions to come.

devo-044.title: The Taghanic event suffocates the shallows
devo-044.text: Trilobites lost an entire order, the Lichida, in the Givetian. The cause was the Taghanic event, an extinction driven by hypoxia, low oxygen, after an anoxic event drained the oceans of oxygen. It sharply cut trilobite diversity, especially in shallow water. One study ranks it as the eighth most ecologically severe mass extinction. Another account places it at the Givetian/Frasnian boundary and credits it with wiping out about half of coral genera.

devo-046.title: Wetlands and the first modern land ecosystems
devo-046.text: Land ecosystems that would look familiar today appeared only in the Late Devonian, about 385 to 359 million years ago. Plants stabilized the edges of fresh water, and the first wetlands developed, with increasingly complex food webs. These wetlands later gave way to the coal forests of the Early Carboniferous.

devo-048.title: The Chilenia terrane docks
devo-048.text: Subduction off western South America kept dragging crust toward the continent. In the Late Devonian it brought a block called the Chilenia terrane into collision with the western border of the Precordillera, where it accreted, welded on for good.

devo-051.title: The Innuitian mountains rise in the Arctic
devo-051.text: Mountains rose across the Canadian Arctic and northernmost Greenland in the Innuitian, or Ellesmere, orogeny. It ran from the Late Devonian into the early Carboniferous. When the range later collapsed, it opened the Sverdrup Basin on Laurussia's northern margin.

devo-052.title: The Late Devonian warms again
devo-052.text: After a cooler middle, the Late Devonian warmed back to Early Devonian levels. More continental weathering and the spread of plants show it. Oddly, carbon dioxide did not rise to match. Arid climates shrank while temperate climates became more common.

devo-047.title: Dead seas make Devonian oil
devo-047.text: The Williston Basin's Bakken shales cover about 520,000 km2 and are a prolific source of oil. They began with suffocated seas. During the Late Devonian extinctions, widespread anoxia halted decay, so organic matter piled up in seafloor mud. Some Bakken layers formed in euxinic waters, without oxygen and full of hydrogen sulfide. Paired with porous reef rocks that hold oil, this made Devonian rocks an important oil source, especially in Canada and the United States.

devo-053.title: The Viluy Traps flood Siberia with basalt
devo-053.text: At the edge of the Siberian Platform, a three-armed rift opened, and deep mantle plumes fed it with lava. These were the Viluy, or Vilyuy, Traps, Siberian flood basalts first erupted in the Late Devonian. The main eruptions ran from about 381 to 366 million years ago, give or take 5 million years, with a later pulse near the end of the Devonian. Dating finds two volcanic phases, the first matching the age of the Kellwasser event. Their role in the extinction is debated. Long thought a major cause of the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, the main eruptions now seem to predate it.

devo-054.title: The Antler orogeny starts the western mountains
devo-054.text: Western North America's long run of mountain building had a beginning. Subduction of Panthalassic ocean floor along Laurussia's western margin drove the Antler orogeny, in the region of the ancestral Sierra Nevada. It began a series of orogenies that culminated in the Laramide. Sources disagree on its start: most say the Late Devonian, but its own article says it began after the Devonian.

devo-055.title: Oxygen settles in the deep sea
devo-055.text: Before about 380 million years ago, oxygen in the deep ocean came and went, sporadic and variable. Only after that date did it stabilize near modern levels.

devo-056.title: Gogo's fossils and the oldest live birth
devo-056.text: In Western Australia, fossils about 380 million years old still show nerves. The Gogo Formation, from the Frasnian, preserves soft tissues in three dimensions, down to embryos with umbilical cords. Those embryos belong to the placoderms Materpiscis, Incisoscutum and Austroptyctodus, the oldest known examples of live birth. Over fifty fish species have been described from Gogo, along with arthropods. Among them is Gogonasus, one of the earliest tetrapodomorphs.

devo-057.title: The buried Kaluga crater
devo-057.text: Under about 800 m of sediment in Russia's Kaluga Oblast lies a crater 15 km across. An impact made it 380 ± 5 million years ago, in the Late Devonian. It is not exposed at the surface.

devo-059.title: The Ilyinets crater
devo-059.text: Ukraine's Ilyinets crater, 8.5 km across, formed about 378 ± 5 million years ago. It is one of several Late Devonian impact scars found in Europe.

devo-058.title: The Alamo impact hits a Nevada sea
devo-058.text: One or more objects traveling at hypervelocity slammed into shallow seas in what is now southeastern Nevada, 377–378 million years ago. It is among the best-exposed and most accurately dated impacts. It came about 5.9 million years before the Frasnian-Famennian extinctions and probably did not affect them. Its age roughly matches the earliest Antler orogeny deposits, and it may have knocked loose huge slide blocks.

devo-060.title: Siljan, Europe's largest impact scar
devo-060.text: A ring of lakes in central Sweden marks the largest impact structure in Europe. A meteorite struck what is now Dalarna and left the Siljan Ring, about 52 km across. The impact is dated to 376.8 ± 1.7 or 377 ± 2 million years ago, in the Frasnian. It was once proposed as a cause of the Kellwasser extinction. That link has weakened, because the extinction has since been dated later, to 371.93–371.78 million years ago.

devo-061.title: The Acadian orogeny raises the Atlantic seaboard
devo-061.text: For about 50 million years from roughly 375 million years ago, mountains grew along North America's Atlantic seaboard. This was the Acadian orogeny, which lasted into the early Mississippian. Its cause was the accretion of Avalonian terranes to Laurentia's eastern margin, most likely starting late in the Early Devonian. Collisions with this crust, broken from Gondwana, closed the southern Iapetus Ocean and raised a high mountain belt between 375 and 359 million years ago. In New England, volcanoes and uplift shed sediment into an inland sea, and {{ref:devo-035}} filled the basin at the mountains' foot. Across the ocean, Acadian squeezing of 404–394 million years ago joined the British Isles into their present shape.

devo-062.title: Tiktaalik, a fish halfway to land
devo-062.text: In Frasnian rocks of Nunavut, Canada, lay a fish with a neck and the makings of limbs. Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish about 375 million years old, had many tetrapod-like features. It bridges fishes such as Panderichthys, about 380 million years old, and early tetrapods such as Acanthostega. Its group, the elpistostegalians, disappeared at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary. There is a twist. If the older {{ref:devo-042}} were made by tetrapods, Tiktaalik's group was an evolutionary dead end, not a direct ancestor.

devo-063.title: The Cerberean Caldera supereruption
devo-063.text: In what is now Victoria, Australia, the Cerberean Caldera is thought to have produced a supereruption about 374 million years ago. It has been suggested as an overlooked contributor to the Kellwasser extinction.

devo-067.title: The Kellwasser event, a Big Five extinction
devo-067.text:
About 70% of species died in the Late Devonian crisis. Its sharpest blow, the Kellwasser event, is named for Germany's Kellwassertal valley and struck at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary. It ranks among the Big Five mass extinctions.

The crisis came in pulses, from the mid-Givetian to the end of the Famennian. Marine life suffered most, and the warm shallow reefs worst of all. Their builders, stromatoporoid sponges and rugose and tabulate corals, were devastated, ending the great reefs of {{ref:devo-041}}. Most remaining jawless fishes died. Placoderms lost much of their diversity. All Frasnian tetrapods vanished, and only two trilobite orders survived.

Why it happened is still uncertain. Suggested causes include anoxia spread by rising seas, global cooling, and nutrient runoff from the roots of new forests, which fed blooms in the sea. Volcanism is debated. The likeliest story may be several causes working together, but researchers have not settled it.

devo-064.title: Magma floods the Dnieper-Donets rift
devo-064.text: A mantle plume drove magmatism in the Dnieper-Donets rift of the East European Platform. It started in the late Frasnian and peaked in the Famennian, when rifting was also most active. This Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets igneous province has been linked to the Frasnian-Famennian extinction.

devo-065.title: The first seeds
devo-065.text: Seeds let plants leave the riverbanks behind. Seed plants first appear in the Famennian, the last Devonian stage, as a sister group to the archaeopteridaleans or to the progymnosperms. A 385-million-year-old seed-plant precursor from Belgium predates them by about 20 million years. By the Famennian, seed plants had already diversified substantially; the earliest seed ferns are Late Devonian lyginopterids. Pollen first appears in the Late Devonian too, still indistinguishable from spores. Seeds sped plants' spread on land and let them exploit uplands away from the water's edge.

devo-066.title: Hyneria, a giant hunter in murky rivers
devo-066.text: Hyneria lindae reached about 2.5–3 meters long, possibly 3.5. This tristichopterid lobe-finned fish hunted Famennian rivers, using large sensory canals to find prey in murky water. It was the largest and most common lobe-fin of Pennsylvania's Red Hill Shale. A second species, up to 2.7 m long, comes from Waterloo Farm in South Africa.

devo-068.title: Large wildfires take hold
devo-068.text: Fire had been possible since the Silurian, but only in the late Famennian did oxygen rise high enough for regular, large-scale wildfires. For the first time, burning became a routine part of life on land.

devo-069.title: Archaeopteris forests change the world
devo-069.text: Archaeopterid trees grew up to 30 m tall, and in the Late Devonian their forests spread rapidly, even onto Gondwana's coasts. Giant Archaeopteris dominated a fairly uniform, low-diversity Famennian flora. Its order, the Archaeopteridales, ranges through the Middle and Late Devonian. These forests had global effects, part of what is called the Late Devonian wood crisis. Trees drew down carbon dioxide, cooling the climate toward the coming ice age. Their deepening roots raised weathering and washed nutrients into the sea, feeding algal blooms that stripped oxygen from deeper waters.

devo-070.title: Cladoselache, an early shark
devo-070.text: Cladoselache appears about 370 million years ago. It was an early shark and the first abundant genus of cartilaginous fish.

devo-072.title: Tree roots teach rivers to meander
devo-072.text: Roots changed the shape of rivers. By 370 million years ago, abundant trees such as Archaeopteris bound soils so firmly that rivers switched from mostly braided, splitting into many channels, to mostly meandering, swinging in single looping channels.

devo-075.title: Acanthostega and Ichthyostega grow legs
devo-075.text:
Acanthostega had legs, lungs and gills, yet its limbs were too weak to carry it on land. That paradox sums up the first tetrapods. Limbed vertebrates such as Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, known from fossils about 365 million years old, were among the earliest able to walk.

Their legs came from fins. In the Famennian, fins with bones and joints became the two pairs of walking legs of the first tetrapods. The oldest Late Devonian tetrapod fossils come from Greenland, but by the end of the period tetrapods lived worldwide, even in high-latitude Gondwana.

The road was not smooth. The Late Devonian extinctions bottlenecked the stem-tetrapods twice, and each time they selected against the most aquatic forms. The survivors were the ones least tied to water, a filter that helped shape the land animals to come.

devo-076.title: Tadpole shrimps, living fossils
devo-076.text: Tadpole shrimps living today, Triops and Lepidurus, look much as their kind has since the end of the Devonian. The oldest known notostracan, Strudops goldenbergi, comes from the Famennian of Belgium, about 365 million years ago.

devo-077.title: The Woodleigh impact structure
devo-077.text: Western Australia's Woodleigh impact structure measures somewhere from 60 to 160 km across. It is dated to 364 ± 8 million years ago, between the Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous. That age roughly matches the Late Devonian extinction.

devo-078.title: Flynn Creek, a well-kept crater
devo-078.text: About 360 million years ago, an object perhaps 90–190 m wide hit a shallow sea in what is now Tennessee. It blasted a crater 3.8 km across and 150 m deep, raised a central hill and shattered rock 200 m down. At least half the broken rock was thrown out. Within a few million years, shales of the Chattanooga Sea buried it, so it is one of the best-preserved ancient impact structures.

devo-081.title: The Late Paleozoic Ice Age begins
devo-081.text: Large ice sheets returned to the land in the Late Devonian and stayed into the Late Permian. The Late Paleozoic Ice Age lasted from about 360 to 255 million years ago. Its first glacial episodes came in the late Famennian and Tournaisian, and the shift from greenhouse to icehouse came in steps. Late Devonian glacial deposits lie in Brazil's Solimoes, Amazonas and Paranaiba basins and in Bolivia, then near the South Pole. Plants burying carbon, along with the uplift of Gondwana, tipped Earth into an icehouse that lasted through the Carboniferous and Permian.

devo-082.title: Waterloo Farm, a fossil coast near the pole
devo-082.text: Near Makhanda, South Africa, a fossil site about 360 million years old opens a window on a near-polar coast. Waterloo Farm, in the Witpoort Formation, is the only record of such an ecosystem, and it overturned assumptions about high latitudes in the latest Devonian. It is the most important Late Devonian fossil site of southern Gondwana.

devo-080.title: The proposed Warburton twin impacts
devo-080.text: Two asteroids 10 km wide may have struck Australia's West and East Warburton Basins, leaving an impact zone 400 km across. The basins have been linked to the Late Devonian extinction, about 360 million years ago. These craters remain hypothetical, proposed but not confirmed.

devo-083.title: The placoderms disappear
devo-083.text: The armored fishes that had ruled Devonian waters did not see the Carboniferous. All placoderms died out in the end-Devonian {{ref:devo-084}}, and no species is confirmed afterward. They had already been reduced in the Kellwasser event. Now the last arthrodires, antiarchs, phyllolepids and ptychodontids vanished abruptly. Their loss opened space for bony and cartilaginous fishes, which radiated in the Carboniferous.

devo-084.title: The Hangenberg event ends the Devonian
devo-084.text:
Two ash beds in Poland pin down a catastrophe. They bracket a black shale at 358.97 ± 0.11 and 358.89 ± 0.20 million years ago, the record of the Hangenberg event, or end-Devonian extinction, which closed the Famennian.

The toll was heavy. It killed the last placoderms and the stromatoporoid reef sponges. It left Proetida as the only trilobite order and nearly wiped out the ammonoids. Most marine and freshwater groups died out or shrank to a few lineages. One estimate ranks it the fourth-deadliest extinction, though land plants were spared.

The likely trigger was cold. Severe cooling and glaciation at the end of the Famennian marked the start of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age and may have driven the losses. Other proposed causes pile up: anoxia from high plankton productivity, volcanism in Kola and Timan-Pechora, ozone loss hinted at by malformed spores, and even a nearby supernova. None is settled, and several may have acted together.

devo-086.title: The last armored jawless fishes
devo-086.text: The jawless armored fishes went out in stages. Osteostracans, galeaspids and heterostracans had died out by the end of the Frasnian. Thelodonts barely made it into the Famennian; the last named, Arianalepis, lived in Iran and Australia. The last ostracoderms became extinct at the end of the Devonian.

devo-087.title: The chitinozoans vanish
devo-087.text: Chitinozoans, microfossils of filter-feeding organisms that drifted in open water, appear to have died out at the end of the Devonian. Rare later finds may be older specimens reworked into younger rocks.

carb-006.title: Cordaitales grow in the coal swamps
carb-006.text: Cordaitales, an order of gymnosperms, seed plants with naked seeds, range from the Carboniferous into the Permian. They took many forms in the coal swamps: tall trees, shrubs, and mangrove-like plants rooted in the wet ground.

carb-007.title: Giant lobe-finned fish rule fresh water
carb-007.text: Rhizodus hibberti, from Great Britain, reached up to 6 m long. It was the largest of the non-tetrapod lobe-finned fish, which were the dominant predators of Carboniferous and Permian fresh waters.

carb-008.title: The Granton Shrimp Bed
carb-008.text: Soft bodies rarely fossilize. Scotland's Granton Shrimp Bed preserves Clydagnathus windsorensis, one of only three conodont species known with its trunk.

carb-009.title: Siberia joins the growing supercontinent
carb-009.text: Siberia had been an independent continent since the early Paleozoic. Then it collided with Kazakhstania, raising the Altai Mountains. The Turkestan Ocean closed, bringing northern Tarim against Kazakhstania from the mid-Carboniferous to the start of the Permian. With Kazakhstania joined to Laurussia, Siberia was effectively part of Pangaea by 310 million years ago, though the blocks kept sliding past each other into the Permian.

openers.middle-devonian-epoch: In the Middle Devonian, Earth grew its first forests. Cladoxylopsid trees stood in the Eifelian, progymnosperms appeared, and the new woods drew carbon from the air and buried it. Reefs of stromatoporoid sponges reached their peak, and in a Polish lagoon something with toes left the oldest tetrapod tracks. But the seas were turning dangerous. The Kačák event raised sea level and spread anoxia, and the Taghanic event followed with another oxygen crisis.
openers.late-devonian-epoch: The Late Devonian was a time of giants, impacts and loss. In Western Australia, the Gogo Formation preserved soft tissues down to nerves and embryos, while deep-sea oxygen finally stabilized near modern levels. Meteorites struck from Russia's Kaluga to Sweden's Siljan Ring, the largest impact structure in Europe. Flood basalts erupted in Siberia, and mountains rose from the Canadian Arctic to the ancestral Sierra Nevada. Underneath it all, oxygen-starved seas buried organic matter, setting up some of the deadliest extinctions in Earth's history.
openers.carboniferous-period: The Carboniferous is the period of coal swamps, and some of its plants, such as the Cordaitales, grew right in them. In fresh water, giant lobe-finned fishes were the top predators. In the rocks of Scotland, a rare bed preserved a conodont with its body intact. And far to the east, Siberia, independent since the early Paleozoic, collided with Kazakhstania and raised the Altai Mountains.

reviews.middle-devonian-epoch: The Middle Devonian's stories meet in the forests. Cladoxylopsid trees and progymnosperms built the first woods, which buried carbon and may explain a cooling of around 5 °C. On land, wetlands with richer food webs followed, and the Catskill Delta preserved the fishes and plants of a world where vertebrates edged ashore, perhaps as early as the Zachełmie tracks. In the sea, stromatoporoid reefs flourished, but the Kačák and Taghanic events showed how quickly warmth and lost oxygen could undo them.
reviews.late-devonian-epoch: The Late Devonian links the rise of trees to the fall of the seas. Archaeopteris forests bound soils, made rivers meander, drew down carbon dioxide and fed nutrients into the oceans, where blooms stripped away oxygen. Those anoxic seas preserved organic matter that became oil, and they helped drive the Kellwasser and Hangenberg extinctions, which ended the reefs, the placoderms and most jawless fishes. Impacts and flood basalts struck too, though most seem mistimed to be the main cause. Through it all, seeds appeared, and limbed tetrapods such as Acanthostega survived bottlenecks that favored forms less tied to water.
reviews.carboniferous-period: The period's opening entries sketch its themes. Cordaitales grew in the coal swamps that give the Carboniferous its name, while lobe-finned fish such as Rhizodus hunted its rivers. Fossil beds like Granton preserved rare soft-bodied animals. And Siberia's collision with Kazakhstania made it effectively part of Pangaea, the supercontinent the period was assembling.
